summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations. The 1951 Penal Code abolished the colonial-era ban, legalising private, adult, non-commercial, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. That revision left no anti-discrimination protection in its place. No statute criminalises gender expression as such, though Human Rights Watch's April 2018 annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region includes Jordan.

Formal decriminalisation does not describe enforcement. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait use public-morality and debauchery provisions in place of explicit criminalisation to harass LGBT people. Vague morality provisions give security forces and private individuals licence to target LGBT people with impunity, and the same research found Jordan's cybercrime and morality laws used to persecute them.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change legal gender markers, in some cases; transgender people cannot. Gender-affirming surgery is permitted for intersex people and criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018, with penalties of up to 10 years' imprisonment. Case No. 2092/2014 concerned a plaintiff born in 1977 who sought a male-to-female change of name and gender in official records after hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, procedures unavailable in Jordan.

Authorities have moved against LGBT organising directly. Human Rights Watch reported on 4 December 2023 that Jordanian officials ran a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality and smeared activists online by sexual orientation, and that social-media users posted activists' photographs with messages inciting violence; two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation. A cybercrime law promulgated in August 2023 could target digital content on gender and sexuality and activists advocating LGBT rights, and security forces intimidated activists with threats of violence, arrest and prosecution, forcing several to shut down organisations, stop activities or flee. CAIRO 52 records that new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access and that security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave the country.

The wider civic-space squeeze reaches online activity. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 chapter of 11 January 2024 records that authorities limited civic space through 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists were arrested and harassed under vague laws, with intrusive digital surveillance. The Press and Publication Law, amended in 1998 and 2004, replaced a ban on depicting sexual perversion with a requirement that the press respect the values of the Arab and Islamic nation.

Social attitudes remain hostile. A 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality. The government tolerates a small number of cafés in Amman widely considered gay-friendly; Books@Cafe, opened in 1997, remains a popular bookstore and café.
tangentialFactors:
Jordan's position sits inside a regional pattern. Human Rights Watch's 6 June 2024 research grouped it with Egypt and Kuwait, where same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in all three states and alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation. The organisation's April 2018 report 'Audacity in Adversity' documents LGBT people speaking out, building alliances and forming regional movements despite state-sponsored repression and stigma.

Medical travel is a practical consequence of the domestic ban: the 2014 case records surgery and hormone therapy obtained in Australia because such procedures are unavailable in Jordan.
localsOnly:
Honour killings as a legal justification for murder were made illegal under the 2013 revised Penal Code. A 2019 Arab Barometer survey found 93% of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality, a figure that shapes family and community responses for residents in ways a short visit does not reach.

Community infrastructure is thin and tolerated rather than protected. The government permits a few cafés in Amman widely considered gay-friendly, among them Books@Cafe, opened in 1997 and still operating as a bookstore and café. My.Kali, the first LGBT publication in the Middle East and North Africa, launched in 2007 and has been online since 2008.
outOfScopeNotes: Several points in the source record are unresolved. OutRight International records that transgender people may change gender markers 'in some cases' without describing the criteria or the authority that decides; no source sets out the procedure, cost or documentary requirements. No published figures record how often Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018 has been enforced, against whom, or whether it has been applied to foreign nationals. Whether the 2023 cybercrime law has been used against visitors, as distinct from residents and activists, is not sourced. The number of transgender and queer people who have left Jordan after community spaces closed is not quantified in the available material.
